segments.t: Meanwhile, Chef Barinov tries to apologize to the television crew after Nagiyev chased them out of the kitchen, but when they consider filming rival chef Elena Pavlovna instead, Viktor refuses to give up his spotlight. Let's listen in Russian.
Вы уж извините, что так вышло.
Виктор Петрович, мы не можем долго ждать.
Я же сказал, договорюсь с Нагиевым.
Now let's examine each line of their conversation and see how the Russian expressions fit together.
Вы уж извините, что так вышло.
'Please forgive me that it turned out this way.' Chef Barinov uses a polite everyday Russian courtesy expression that sets the tone of the conversation right away.
'I will talk to Nagiyev.' Chef Viktor uses the first-person pronoun in the case required by the Russian verb or preposition.
'In a day or two he will cool down.' Notice how Russian puts 'day' and 'to cool down, go cold' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
Виктор Петрович, мы не можем долго ждать.
'Viktor Petrovich, we cannot wait that long.' Here Elena anchors the thought on 'can' and finishes on 'to wait, to expect', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
'Our deadlines are burning.' Russians say 'by me' or 'with us' where English says 'I have' or 'we have', without needing a separate word for 'have'.
'We will find someone else.' Elena pairs 'will find' with 'other, another, different' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.
'Who else?' In spoken Russian, the words stay in their normal statement order and Chef Barinov's rising voice at the end turns the line into a question.
'Well, we will find somebody.' Elena centers this short reply on 'will find', letting a few direct words carry the whole meaning.
'She is also a very famous chef.' In everyday Russian, 'also, too' flows straight into 'cook' without extra linking words.
'There is no need to ask anyone else.' Chef Barinov pairs 'need to, must' with 'to ask, to beg' directly, since spoken Russian skips English filler words like 'the', 'a', and 'is'.
Я же сказал, договорюсь с Нагиевым.
'I told you, I will make a deal with Nagiyev.' Notice how Russian puts 'said' and 'nagiyev' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
'Well, all right then.' Elena centers this short reply on 'good, well, all right', letting a few direct words carry the whole meaning. Now let's replay the whole dialogue at natural speed.
Вы уж извините, что так вышло.
Виктор Петрович, мы не можем долго ждать.
Я же сказал, договорюсь с Нагиевым.
That completes Chef Barinov's tense negotiation with the television director over their tight deadline. Listen out for how Russian speakers talk about time pressure and making deals. Until next time!
